title: Online Indonesian — slang, shorthand and acronyms
goal: Read Indonesian as it is actually typed: Gen-Z slang on social media, vowel-less chat shorthand, and the acronyms that fill every official message. You will also learn the official Indonesian words for the internet things everyone calls by English names.
bekal: understand common slang and chat forms: *gabut, mager, baper, santuy, spill, gpp, otw, btw, wkwk*
decode acronyms and abbreviations such as *Pemda, ASN, Puskesmas, Jabodetabek* and tell a *singkatan* from an *akronim*
choose between a relaxed caption and a formal one, and use *unggahan, tautan, tagar* in official text

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Akun Instagram program
dialogs.intro: Yoga, now a junior staffer, runs the programme's Instagram account. One Thursday afternoon in May he shows Sarah the caption for the next day's post, which promotes next year's registration.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Mbak, caption buat unggahan besok udah aku draf. Mau cek dulu?
lines.id: I've drafted the caption for tomorrow's post. Do you want to check it first?
lines.literal: Miss, caption for upload tomorrow already I draft. want check first?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Boleh. Coba bacakan.
lines.id: Sure. Read it out.
lines.literal: may. try read-for.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: “Siapa yang masih gabut akhir pekan ini? Spill rencana kalian di kolom komentar!”
lines.id: “Who's still bored with nothing to do this weekend? Spill your plans in the comments!”
lines.literal: who that still idle end week this? spill plan you-all at column comment!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Gabut itu apa? Aku tahunya cuma mager.
lines.id: What's “gabut”? I only know “mager”.
lines.literal: gabut that what? I know-its only mager.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Gabut itu nggak ada kerjaan, bosan. Kalau mager, malas gerak.
lines.id: “Gabut” is having nothing to do, being bored. “Mager” is too lazy to move.
lines.literal: gabut that not exist work, bored. if mager, lazy move.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke. Tapi ini akun resmi program, Yog. Sasaran kita guru dan kepala sekolah juga.
lines.id: OK. But this is the programme's official account, Yog. Our audience includes teachers and head teachers too.
lines.literal: OK. but this account official programme, Yog. target our teacher and head school also.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Justru itu, Mbak. Kalau terlalu kaku, anak muda nggak mau baca.
lines.id: That's exactly it. If it's too stiff, young people won't read it.
lines.literal: precisely that, Miss. if too stiff, child young not want read.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Setuju. Tapi jangan sampai kepala sekolah di Kupang bingung baca “spill”.
lines.id: Agreed. But we can't have a head teacher in Kupang puzzling over “spill”.
lines.literal: agree. but don't until head school at Kupang confused read spill.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Gimana kalau dua gaya? Slide pertama santuy, slide kedua lengkap dan baku.
lines.id: What about two styles? First slide chilled, second slide complete and formal.
lines.literal: how if two style? slide first relaxed, slide second complete and standard.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, itu ide bagus. Sertakan juga tautan pendaftaran dan tenggatnya.
lines.id: Now that's a good idea. Include the registration link and the deadline too.
lines.literal: [nah], that idea good. include also link registration and deadline-its.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap. Tagarnya tetap #JembatanAusIndo, ya?
lines.id: Will do. The hashtag stays #JembatanAusIndo, right?
lines.literal: ready. hashtag-the still #JembatanAusIndo, [ya]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tetap. Satu lagi: jangan pakai “wkwk” kalau membalas komentar orang yang komplain.
lines.id: Yes. One more thing: no “wkwk” when you reply to people who've complained.
lines.literal: still. one more: don't use wkwk if reply comment person who complain.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Hehe, iya, Mbak. Itu mah bikin orang tambah baper.
lines.id: Heh, yes. That just makes people even more upset.
lines.literal: hehe, yes, Miss. that [mah] make person more baper.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, “baper” aku ngerti. Bawa perasaan, kan?
lines.id: Now “baper” I understand. Taking things to heart, right?
lines.literal: [nah], baper I understand. carry feeling, [kan]?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Betul. Wah, Mbak Sarah makin gaul.
lines.id: Right. Wow, you're getting really down with the kids.
lines.literal: correct. wow, Miss Sarah increasingly sociable-cool.

notes: **Gabut vs mager.** *Mager* is *malas gerak*, "too lazy to move" — a choice. *Gabut* began as *gaji buta*, "blind salary", pay for doing nothing, and now means "idle, bored, with nothing to do" — a situation. You can be *gabut* at your desk; you are *mager* on the sofa.

**Spill and the English inside Indonesian.** *Spill* ("spill the tea") means "reveal the details": *Spill dong!* — "Tell us everything!". Young urban Indonesians mix English in freely, a style nicknamed *bahasa anak Jaksel* (South Jakarta kids' language), with its famous *which is* and *literally*. It is fashionable, and also a running joke.

**Baper, santuy, gaul.** *Baper* = *bawa perasaan*, "to take things personally, get over-emotional". *Santuy* is a playful twist of *santai* (relaxed). *Gaul* means "sociable, trendy, in the know"; *bahasa gaul* is the umbrella term for all of this slang.

**Unggahan, tautan, tagar.** These are the official Indonesian words for upload (post), link and hashtag, coined by the Language Agency (Badan Bahasa). In speech people say *posting, link, hashtag*; in an official caption, a letter or a report, the Indonesian terms look professional. A caption itself can be *keterangan*, or the new word *takarir*.

**Wkwk.** Typed laughter, from the sound of a wheezy laugh: *wkwk, wkwkwk*, the mock-typo *awokawok*, as well as *haha* and the giggly *xixixi*. It is friendly among friends, but under a complaint it reads as mockery — Sarah's rule is sound.

**Itu mah, jangan sampai.** *Mah* is a Sundanese topic particle ("as for that…") heard all over Jakarta. *Jangan sampai* means "let's make sure it doesn't come to…" — a handy way to warn about an outcome rather than an action: *Jangan sampai terlambat* ("make sure we're not late").

grammars.title: How slang words are made
body: Indonesian slang is mostly built from the language's own raw material. Once you know the recipes, new words become guessable.
after: *Healing* in Indonesian slang means a trip or break to recover from stress — *Weekend ini mau healing ke Puncak* — not medical treatment. It is a good example of an English loan changing meaning on arrival.

grammars.title: Chat shorthand
body: In chat, Indonesians drop vowels, keep the consonant skeleton, and borrow English initials. These seven cover a surprising share of any group chat.
after: ⚠️ *Otw* officially means "on the way"; in practice it often means "about to leave" or "just getting in the shower". Indonesians joke about *otw* the way Britons joke about "five minutes away".

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Membaca grup WhatsApp
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning, the day of a workshop for partner schools. Messages are pouring into the coordinators' WhatsApp group, and Sarah asks Fajar to decode them with her.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Fajar, tolong bantu. Pak Joko nulis: “Mhn maaf, sy blm bs hadir, msh rapat di Pemda.”
lines.id: Fajar, help me out. Pak Joko writes: “Apologies, I can't attend yet, still in a meeting at the Pemda.”
lines.literal: Fajar, please help. Mr Joko write: ask sorry, I not-yet can attend, still meeting at Pemda.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Gampang, Mbak. “Mohon maaf, saya belum bisa hadir, masih rapat di pemerintah daerah.”
lines.id: Easy. “Apologies, I can't attend yet, I'm still in a meeting at the local government office.”
lines.literal: easy, Miss. ask sorry, I not-yet can attend, still meeting at government region.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke. Terus ini: “Guru2 ASN wajib izin ke Disdik dulu.”
lines.id: OK. And this one: “ASN teachers must get permission from the Disdik first.”
lines.literal: OK. then this: teacher-teacher ASN obliged permission to Disdik first.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: ASN itu aparatur sipil negara, pegawai negeri. Disdik itu dinas pendidikan.
lines.id: ASN is the state civil apparatus, civil servants. Disdik is the education office.
lines.literal: ASN that apparatus civil state, employee state. Disdik that service education.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Masuk akal. Yang ini: “Btw peserta dr Bekasi otw, tp macet parah se-Jabodetabek wkwk.”
lines.id: Makes sense. This one: “Btw the Bekasi participants are otw, but the whole of Jabodetabek is gridlocked lol.”
lines.literal: enter reason. which this: btw participant from Bekasi otw, but jam severe all-Jabodetabek wkwk.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Jabodetabek: Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, Bekasi. Satu kawasan, satu macet.
lines.id: Jabodetabek: Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, Bekasi. One region, one traffic jam.
lines.literal: Jabodetabek: Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, Bekasi. one area, one jam.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dan “otw” artinya mereka sudah di jalan?
lines.id: And “otw” means they're already on the road?
lines.literal: and otw meaning-its they already at road?

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Secara teori, Mbak. Secara praktik, bisa jadi baru mandi.
lines.id: In theory. In practice, they may have just got in the shower.
lines.literal: in-manner theory, Miss. in-manner practice, can become just bathe.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Astaga. Yang terakhir: “Ada peserta demam, sdh dibawa ke Puskesmas.”
lines.id: Good grief. The last one: “One participant has a fever, already taken to the Puskesmas.”
lines.literal: good-grief. which last: exist participant fever, already is-brought to Puskesmas.

lines.speaker: Fajar:
lines.text: Pusat kesehatan masyarakat. Tenang, Mbak, ada di tiap kecamatan.
lines.id: Community health centre. Don't worry, there's one in every district.
lines.literal: centre health society. calm, Miss, exist at every district.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Syukurlah. Aku balas tanpa singkatan: “Terima kasih infonya, Pak. Semoga lekas sembuh.”
lines.id: Thank goodness. I'll reply without abbreviations: “Thank you for letting us know. We hope they get well soon.”
lines.literal: thankfully. I reply without abbreviation: thank you info-the, Sir. hopefully quickly recover.

notes: **Mhn, sy, blm, bs, msh, dr, tp, sdh.** Chat shorthand keeps the consonants and drops the vowels. Interestingly, the heaviest abbreviators are often older professionals like Pak Joko: the content is polite (*Mohon maaf*), the spelling telegraphic. Don't copy it in anything formal, and don't read it as rudeness.

**Guru2.** The number 2 for reduplication is a typewriter-era habit still alive in chat and handwritten notes: *guru2, anak2, hati2 di jalan*. In any formal text write the full form with a hyphen: *guru-guru*.

**ASN.** *Aparatur sipil negara* is the umbrella term for state employees, covering the older *PNS* (*pegawai negeri sipil*) and contract staff. Teachers at state schools are often ASN, which is why they need official permission (*izin*) to attend events in working hours.

**Pemda, Disdik.** Many institution names are shortened by taking the first syllable or two of each word: *pemerintah daerah → Pemda*, *dinas pendidikan → Disdik*, *dinas kesehatan → Dinkes*. Once you know the full phrases, you can decode new ones yourself.

**Jabodetabek.** Greater Jakarta, home to more than 30 million people. The acronym grew with the suburbs: it was *Jabotabek* until Depok became a city in 1999 and claimed its *-de-*. *Macet parah* ("a terrible jam") is the phrase most often typed in it.

**Puskesmas, kecamatan, semoga lekas sembuh.** A *Puskesmas* is the state community health centre, one in every *kecamatan* (district, the level below a regency or city). *Semoga lekas sembuh* — "hope you get well soon" — is the standard wish; *cepat sembuh ya* is the casual version.

grammars.title: Singkatan or akronim?
body: Indonesian grammar distinguishes two kinds of shortening. A *singkatan* is read letter by letter; an *akronim* is pronounced as a word. The difference matters when you say them aloud.
after: Acronyms that have become ordinary nouns are written in lower case (*balita, rudal, tilang*); those naming one specific institution keep a capital (*Bappenas, Pemda DKI*). Letters in a *singkatan* are said with Indonesian letter names: *é* for E, *ha* for H, *ka* for K.

blocks.text: Official Indonesia runs on acronyms. These appear on forms, in the news and in every bureaucratic conversation; knowing the full form tells you what the thing actually is.
*SIM* shows why the distinction matters: as a *singkatan* you might expect "és-i-ém", but everyone pronounces it as a word, *SIM*. Usage wins; when in doubt, listen to how people say it.

Ministries rename themselves after almost every change of government, and their acronyms change with them. If an acronym beginning with *Kemen-* (*kementerian*, ministry) looks unfamiliar, search the full name rather than guessing: the pattern is always *Kemen-* plus the first syllables of the portfolio, as in *Kemenkes* (health) or *Kemenlu* (foreign affairs).
Slang ages fast, and some of these words will sound dated by the time you read this. They are still worth recognising, because they fill comment sections and group chats.
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.
